newsitem.title: USA: Ahmanson, Great Western face off in court Friday.
newsitem.headline: Ahmanson, Great Western face off in court Friday.

text.p: H.F. Ahmanson and Co., which is running out of time in the takeover battle for Great Western Financial Corp., will try to derail Washington Mutual Inc.'s proposed $6.75 billion acquisition of Great Western in court Friday.

Delaware Chancery Court in Wilmington, Del., has set a hearing on a request by Ahmanson, the Irwindale, Calif.-based parent of Home Savings of America, to delay a shareholder vote set for June 13 on Washington Mutual's proposal for a friendly merger with Great Western, which would create the largest thrift in the country, with assets of about $86 billion.
"It's one of the last opportunities for Ahmanson to block the Washington Mutual transaction," said Thomas Theurkauf, analyst with Keefe Bruyette Woods.

Ahmanson, whose bid is valued at $6.6 billion, is seeking the delay, claiming Great Western violated its bylaws by setting a shareholder vote on the same day as a meeting to elect new directors to the board.
Ahmanson is trying to get three people backing its bid elected to the board.
Legal experts close to the situation said a court decision could come as soon as Friday but is more likely next week. One legal expert said either side was likely to appeal an unfavourable ruling.
Analysts said Ahmanson stands a lot to lose if the court rules against it.

"If Ahmanson does not prevail in creating a delay, then the Washington Mutual deal will go to the shareholder vote. The consensus view is Washington has the upper hand in the (takeover battle) and is the odds-on favourite to win," Theurkauf said. "I think the odds are at least 80-20 Washington will win."
Others said the odds would not change much even if Ahmanson prevails in court, although it would buy time.

"A favourable ruling for Ahmanson in court would not change the financial dynamics of the deal. The market is valuing Washington Mutual as the winner," said Campbell Chaney, analyst with Sandler O'Neill.

Analysts said investors are favouring Seattle-based Washington Mutual's bid because it is a friendly transaction endorsed by Great Western's board and because of Washington Mutual Chairman Kerry Killinger's reputation and success in executing acquisitions, a total of 22 in the last 10 years.
In a recent interview, Killinger said he was confident Washington Mutual would proceed with the merger even if Ahmanson tries to raise its bid.

Ahmanson launched a hostile bid in February for Chatsworth, Calif.-based Great Western and has been fighting to complete the deal despite Great Western's rejection of the offer and its merger agreement, announced on March 6, with white knight Washington Mutual.
Ahmanson raised its bid and is now offering up to 1.2 of its shares for each Great Western share, while Washington Mutual's deal calls for an exchange of 0.9 of a share for each Great Western share.
Based on Thursday's prices, Ahmanson's bid was valued at $47.40 a share, or about $6.6 billion, while Washington Mutual's bid was worth $48.49 a share, or about $6.75 billion.
Ahmanson was unchanged at $39.50 while Great Western rose 12.5 cents to $46.50, both on the New York Stock Exchange. Washington Mutual fell 18.75 cents to $53.875 on Nasdaq.
Analysts said one of Ahmanson's few remaining options was to sweeten its bid again.

"One of the strong suits for Ahmanson is their credibility in the investment community and if they sweeten their proposal meaningfully, there could be an investor backlash. They have to make sure the economics make sense or they could wind up hurting their chances," Chaney said.
Ahmanson has declined to comment on whether it would raise its bid. A source close to the company admitted, however, that there are concerns that raising its bid again would not help.
"There's no reason to believe that any bid we put on the table would get a different reaction," the source said.
Ahmanson has argued its proposal has far more cost-cutting potential because both Ahmanson and Great Western are based in the Los Angeles area.
Several analysts believe Ahmanson will become a takeover target if it fails.
